entry.title: Postal codes and tessellations
entry.content: ## From postal points to areas using Voronoi polygons ![](https://dieghernan.github.io/assets/img/blog/2026-11-06-postal-codes-slovenia-postal-codes-1.webp) I recently published my project [Postal codes of Spain](https://dieghernan.github.io/codigospostales/), with estimated postal areas, an interactive map and GeoPackage downloads. But there is something we have not looked at yet: how do those address points become polygons? The answer is... **Voronoi polygons**. ## What is a Voronoi polygon? Imagine a few shops on a flat map. Which one is closest to your house? Ask that question for every location and give each shop its own color. The result is a **Voronoi diagram**, also known as a **Voronoi tessellation**, **Voronoi decomposition**, **Voronoi partition** or **Dirichlet tessellation**. This technique divides a plane into regions based on the distance to a given set of points. In our example, each shop is a **site**, or generating point. Its **Voronoi cell**, also called a **Thiessen polygon**, contains the locations at least as close to that site as to any other. Along a shared edge, two sites are equally close. Where several cells meet, there may be a tie between more sites. With ordinary straight-line distance, the edges follow perpendicular bisectors between sites. Some cells extend indefinitely, so maps usually show them clipped to a study area. The name honors Georgy Voronoi, who studied these partitions in the early twentieth century. The idea has earlier roots, including Dirichlet's nineteenth-century work (hence the name Dirichlet tessellation). [Pokojski and Pokojska (2018)](https://doi.org/10.2478/pcr-2018-0009) review the history and geographical applications. These partitions are useful for exploring proximity to shops or public services, assigning areas to weather stations and studying spatial patterns. For example, Thiessen polygons can supply area weights when estimating rainfall from rain gauges. The underlying question is always about the chosen distance: the nearest hospital in a straight line may not be the quickest one to reach. ### A tiny example in **R** Let's start with five points in an imaginary square, including one at its center, using just **sf** and **ggplot2**. The coordinates have arbitrary units and no geographical coordinate reference system. ```r library(sf) library(ggplot2) # Define a common theme for the maps. background <- "#faf8f2" ink <- "#203b47" theme_set( theme_void() + theme( plot.background = element_rect(fill = background, colour = NA), panel.background = element_rect(fill = background, colour = NA), plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink), plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = ink), plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", hjust = 0), legend.position = "bottom", plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10) ) ) sites <- data.frame( site = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"), x = c(2, 7, 3, 8, 5), y = c(2, 3, 8, 7, 5) ) toy_points <- st_as_sf(sites, coords = c("x", "y")) study_area <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(c(xmin = 0, ymin = 0, xmax = 10, ymax = 10))) toy_cells <- toy_points |> st_union() |> st_voronoi(envelope = study_area) |> st_collection_extract("POLYGON") |> st_intersection(study_area) ggplot() + geom_sf( data = toy_cells, fill = c("#a8dadc", "#f4c89a", "#c6b8df", "#bfd59b", "#f2b5c4"), colour = "white", linewidth = 1 ) + geom_sf(data = toy_points, colour = "#203b47", size = 3) + geom_text( data = sites, aes(x, y, label = site), nudge_y = 0.5, colour = "#203b47", fontface = "bold" ) + coord_sf(datum = NA) + labs( title = "Five points, five Voronoi cells", subtitle = "Each location belongs to the closest site" ) ``` Five points, five cells. The point E at `(5, 5)` has a bounded cell surrounded by the other four. The outer cells extend beyond the square and are clipped to its edges. `st_union()` collects the points into one geometry, `st_voronoi()` builds the diagram and `st_intersection()` clips it to our square. The colors help us tell the cells apart. We have not assigned any postal codes yet. The diagram knows nothing about roads, rivers or administrative boundaries. As we move to postal points, we will need to make our choices about those boundaries explicit. ## Before we start: what are we estimating? The Spanish project uses CartoCiudad address points with their postal codes. It follows [Goerlich (2022)](https://doi.org/10.12842/WPIVIE_0322), who develops an idea presented by [Sánchez (2020)](https://www.nosolosig.com/articulos/asi-hice-el-mapa-de-los-codigos-postales-de-espana-con-sig-y-datos-abiertos). The [updated online version](https://www.uv.es/goerlich/Ivie/CodPost.html) describes the method in detail. For Slovenia, we will use GISCO's postal points, retrieved with **giscoR**. There is an important difference here: a representative point for a code tells us much less than thousands of addresses with that code. Detailed addresses help the partition follow their distribution more closely, although proximity alone still cannot reproduce postal delivery decisions. We have not established that Slovenian postal areas should follow municipal boundaries. Imposing those boundaries is a modeling choice for this exercise, inspired by the Spanish workflow, rather than a verified property of the Slovenian postal system. This post explains the workflow. The polygons we create are not official postal boundaries, and this exercise does not validate the GISCO postal data. {: .alert .alert-warning .p-3 .mx-2 .mb-3} ## Getting the data First, let's get the municipal boundaries and postal points. We use the 2024 release of both datasets. ```r library(giscoR) library(sf) library(dplyr) municipalities <- gisco_get_lau( year = 2024, country = "SI", epsg = 3035 ) |> select(GISCO_ID, LAU_NAME) |> st_make_valid() raw_points <- gisco_get_postalcodes( year = 2024, country = "SI", epsg = 3035 ) ``` We work in **ETRS89 / LAEA Europe (EPSG:3035)**, a projected coordinate system with coordinates in meters. This makes the 200 m and 50 m margins used later meaningful. Voronoi uses Euclidean distances in this plane, rather than road distances. The projection does not preserve every distance exactly either. Before we start drawing, what have we actually downloaded? ```r postal_points <- raw_points |> mutate(POSTCODE = trimws(as.character(POSTCODE))) |> filter(!is.na(POSTCODE), POSTCODE != "") |> select(POSTCODE) code_counts <- postal_points |> st_drop_geometry() |> count(POSTCODE, name = "points_per_code") knitr::kable(data.frame( Indicator = c( "Municipalities", "Downloaded points", "Points with a postal code", "Distinct postal codes", "Codes represented by one point" ), Value = c( nrow(municipalities), nrow(raw_points), nrow(postal_points), nrow(code_counts), sum(code_counts$points_per_code == 1) ) )) ``` | Indicator | Value | | :----------------------------- | ----: | | Municipalities | 212 | | Downloaded points | 557 | | Points with a postal code | 557 | | Distinct postal codes | 557 | | Codes represented by one point | 557 | These counts give us a first look at the file, but they are not a quality check. They do not establish whether every code is present or whether the coordinates are correct. With one point per code, we will be drawing areas around representatives rather than estimating them from individual addresses. Two points at exactly the same coordinates cannot generate separate Voronoi cells. We sort by postal code and keep the first point at each location, as in the original workflow. This is a reproducible tie-breaking rule, not evidence that the retained code is correct. The counts below show how many records we remove and how many locations have conflicting codes. ```r postal_points <- postal_points |> arrange(POSTCODE) conflicts <- postal_points |> group_by(geometry) |> summarise(codes = n_distinct(POSTCODE), .groups = "drop") |> filter(codes > 1) duplicates <- duplicated(postal_points$geometry) knitr::kable(data.frame( Indicator = c("Duplicate locations removed", "Locations with conflicting codes"), Value = c(sum(duplicates), nrow(conflicts)) )) ``` | Indicator | Value | | :------------------------------- | ----: | | Duplicate locations removed | 79 | | Locations with conflicting codes | 16 | ```r postal_points <- postal_points[!duplicates, ] ``` ## Starting with Ljubljana Let's pick Ljubljana and keep the points inside it. We use `st_within()` so that a point exactly on a shared boundary is not assigned to both neighboring municipalities. ```r city <- municipalities |> filter(LAU_NAME == "Ljubljana") city_points <- st_filter(postal_points, city, .predicate = st_within) base_map <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = city, fill = "#e8e4d8", colour = ink, linewidth = 0.4) gisco_attr <- gisco_attributions() base_map + geom_sf(data = city_points, colour = "#bd5137", size = 2) + labs( title = "Ljubljana: the starting point", subtitle = "A municipal boundary and points with postal codes", caption = gisco_attr ) ``` ### Building the cells Each cell contains locations at least as close to its generating point as to any other point. Cell boundaries occur where distances to two points are equal. For this first demonstration, we keep all interior points, without the margins used in the national workflow. ```r cells <- city_points |> st_union() |> st_voronoi(envelope = st_as_sfc(st_bbox(city))) |> st_collection_extract("POLYGON") |> st_sf(geometry = _) base_map + geom_sf(data = cells, fill = NA, colour = "#bd5137", linewidth = 0.5) + geom_sf(data = city_points, colour = ink, size = 2) + labs( title = "An area of proximity for every point", subtitle = "Cells still extend beyond the municipal boundary", caption = "Own elaboration using data from Eurostat / GISCO, 2024" ) ``` `st_union()` gathers the points so we build one diagram. One detail to keep in mind: `envelope` supplies a working extent, but **does not clip** the cells to the municipality. We need an intersection for that. ### Clipping and recovering postal codes It would be convenient if cells came out in the same order as the input points, but we should not rely on that. Instead, we recover each cell's code with a spatial relationship before clipping. Each cell must contain exactly one generating point. ```r point_matches <- st_intersects(cells, city_points) cells$POSTCODE <- city_points$POSTCODE[unlist(point_matches)] clipped_geometry <- st_intersection(st_geometry(cells), st_geometry(city)) city_cells <- st_sf( POSTCODE = cells$POSTCODE[attr(clipped_geometry, "idx")[, 1]], geometry = clipped_geometry ) city_areas <- city_cells |> group_by(POSTCODE) |> summarise(.groups = "drop") |> st_make_valid() city_colours <- setNames( hcl.colors(nrow(city_areas), palette = "Dark 3"), sort(city_areas$POSTCODE) ) city_labels <- st_sf( POSTCODE = city_areas$POSTCODE, geometry = st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(city_areas)) ) ggplot(city_areas) + geom_sf(aes(fill = POSTCODE), colour = background, linewidth = 0.6) + geom_sf( data = city_points, shape = 21, fill = ink, colour = background, size = 2.4 ) + geom_sf_text( data = city_labels, aes(label = POSTCODE), colour = ink, fontface = "bold", size = 3.5 ) + scale_fill_manual(values = city_colours, guide = "none") + coord_sf(datum = NA) + labs( title = "From points to estimated areas", subtitle = "Cells clipped and merged by postal code", caption = "Teaching example · Not official postal boundaries" ) ``` We intersect the geometry columns, then use the intersection's `idx` matrix to recover each cell's postal code. This keeps the attribute assignment explicit. Label positions are also calculated from geometries alone. Grouping by postal code with `summarise()` merges the geometries. With many addresses sharing a code, their cells would dissolve into one geometry, possibly with several separate parts. ## From one municipality to the whole country Ljubljana is done. Now let's repeat the operation for each component of each municipality. Municipalities can have separate pieces: normalizing to `MULTIPOLYGON` and then casting to `POLYGON` lets us handle them independently, without automatically extending a code to a piece with no points. The municipality ID and name apply to every component, so we mark those attributes as spatially constant before splitting the geometries. ```r components <- municipalities |> st_set_agr("constant") |> st_cast("MULTIPOLYGON") |> st_cast("POLYGON") |> mutate(component_id = row_number()) ``` ### Why use an inward margin? In the Spanish project, we first select addresses within an inward margin of **200 m**. If none are found, we try **50 m**. This reduces the influence of points close to a boundary, where small mismatches between layers may affect their assignment. There is no universal rule behind these numbers. Goerlich describes a 20 m margin. The 200 m and 50 m choices come from my implementation. We keep them here to explain that workflow, although sparse postal points make it easier to exclude useful information. Comparing other margins would be a useful next step. ```r select_points <- function(component, postal_points) { for (margin in c(200, 50)) { interior <- st_buffer(st_geometry(component), -margin) if (all(st_is_empty(interior))) next selected_points <- st_filter(postal_points, interior, .predicate = st_within ) if (nrow(selected_points) > 0) { return(selected_points) } } postal_points[0, ] } ``` The margin only selects points: the resulting areas cover the **original** component, not the smaller buffered geometry. If both attempts fail, we leave the component unassigned. We do not borrow the nearest point from outside the municipality. ### Three cases, one function There are three cases to handle. With no points, we keep the component and assign `NA`. If all selected points share a code, we assign it to the whole component. We only need Voronoi when several codes are present: no need to split an area that already has a single assignment. ```r build_areas <- function(component, postal_points) { selected_points <- select_points(component, postal_points) codes <- unique(selected_points$POSTCODE) if (length(codes) <= 1L) { component$POSTCODE <- if (length(codes)) codes else NA_character_ return(component) } cells <- selected_points |> st_union() |> st_voronoi(envelope = st_as_sfc(st_bbox(component))) |> st_collection_extract("POLYGON") |> st_sf(geometry = _) point_matches <- st_intersects(cells, selected_points) cells$POSTCODE <- selected_points$POSTCODE[unlist(point_matches)] clipped_geometry <- st_intersection( st_geometry(cells), st_geometry(component) ) result <- st_sf( POSTCODE = cells$POSTCODE[attr(clipped_geometry, "idx")[, 1]], geometry = clipped_geometry ) |> group_by(POSTCODE) |> summarise(.groups = "drop") |> st_make_valid() result$GISCO_ID <- component$GISCO_ID result$LAU_NAME <- component$LAU_NAME result$component_id <- component$component_id result } result <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(components)), function(i) { build_areas(components[i, ], postal_points) }) |> bind_rows() ``` ### Handling unassigned areas Can we fill any of the gaps? A component without points may belong to a municipality whose other components have information. We recover its code only if the municipality has **one distinct recovered code**. This is an imputation from the available data, not proof that the municipality really has just one code. ```r unique_codes <- result |> st_drop_geometry() |> filter(!is.na(POSTCODE)) |> distinct(GISCO_ID, POSTCODE) |> add_count(GISCO_ID) |> filter(n == 1) unassigned_before <- sum(is.na(result$POSTCODE)) index <- match(result$GISCO_ID, unique_codes$GISCO_ID) recoverable <- is.na(result$POSTCODE) & !is.na(index) result$POSTCODE[recoverable] <- unique_codes$POSTCODE[index[recoverable]] ``` Before drawing the final map, let's tidy up the geometries and keep only surfaces. Repairs can produce collections containing residual lines or points, which do not belong in an area layer. Dissolving by postal code also removes municipal boundaries between areas sharing that code. ```r keep_surfaces <- function(x) { geometry <- st_make_valid(st_geometry(x)) geometry <- lapply(geometry, function(part) { if (!inherits(part, c("POLYGON", "MULTIPOLYGON", "GEOMETRYCOLLECTION"))) { return(st_multipolygon()) } surfaces <- suppressWarnings(st_collection_extract(st_sfc(part), "POLYGON")) if (length(surfaces) == 0L || all(st_is_empty(surfaces))) { return(st_multipolygon()) } st_cast(st_union(surfaces), "MULTIPOLYGON", warn = FALSE)[[1]] }) st_geometry(x) <- st_sfc(geometry, crs = st_crs(x)) x[!st_is_empty(x), ] } unassigned <- result |> filter(is.na(POSTCODE)) |> keep_surfaces() postal_areas <- result |> filter(!is.na(POSTCODE)) |> group_by(POSTCODE) |> summarise(.groups = "drop") |> keep_surfaces() |> st_cast("MULTIPOLYGON") ``` ## The complete map For the national overview, let's color the areas by the first digit of their code. This keeps the map readable, without claiming that we have validated a classification of postal regions. Gray is reserved for unassigned components, with their own legend entry. ```r postal_colours <- c( "1" = "#007F7F", "2" = "#E87500", "3" = "#3B6FB6", "4" = "#A64E9A", "5" = "#649A32", "6" = "#D9AF00", "8" = "#B94350", "9" = "#6255A4", "Unassigned" = "#727A80" ) postal_groups <- sort(unique(substr(postal_areas$POSTCODE, 1, 1))) ggplot() + geom_sf(data = municipalities, fill = "#d5d2ca", colour = NA) + geom_sf( data = postal_areas, aes(fill = substr(POSTCODE, 1, 1)), colour = background, linewidth = 0.15 ) + geom_sf( data = unassigned, aes(fill = "Unassigned"), colour = background, linewidth = 0.15 ) + scale_fill_manual( values = postal_colours, name = "Postal code group", breaks = c(postal_groups, "Unassigned"), labels = c(paste0(postal_groups, "xxx"), "Unassigned") ) + coord_sf(datum = NA) + labs( title = "Slovenia, point by point", subtitle = "Proximity areas clipped to municipal boundaries", caption = paste("Eurostat / GISCO, 2024 · Own elaboration", "Dark grey: unassigned areas · Estimated boundaries, not official", sep = "\n" ) ) ``` ## Checking the result The map is ready, but let's check the geometry before going further. Are the polygons valid? Do assigned and unassigned areas cover the territory? Are there any appreciable overlaps? We allow one square meter for numerical differences in the geometry operations. ```r territory <- st_union(st_geometry(municipalities)) coverage <- st_union(c(st_geometry(postal_areas), st_geometry(unassigned))) difference_m2 <- as.numeric(sum(st_area(st_sym_difference(territory, coverage)))) overlap_m2 <- as.numeric( sum(st_area(postal_areas)) + sum(st_area(unassigned)) - sum(st_area(coverage)) ) knitr::kable(data.frame( Indicator = c( "Codes with an estimated area", "Components assigned by municipal recovery", "Unassigned records", "Unassigned area (km²)", "Coverage difference (m²)", "Overlap (m²)" ), Value = round(c( nrow(postal_areas), sum(recoverable), nrow(unassigned), as.numeric(sum(st_area(unassigned))) / 1e6, difference_m2, overlap_m2 ), 4) )) ``` | Indicator | Value | | :---------------------------------------- | -------: | | Codes with an estimated area | 468.0000 | | Components assigned by municipal recovery | 4.0000 | | Unassigned records | 6.0000 | | Unassigned area (km²) | 150.2033 | | Coverage difference (m²) | 0.0000 | | Overlap (m²) | -0.0002 | These checks verify the geometry, **not postal accuracy**. We could cover an entire country with valid polygons and still have a poor approximation of its delivery areas. ## Back to Spain We now have the full sequence: points, proximity areas, clipping and merging by postal code. The same steps work with much more detailed addresses, such as the CartoCiudad data in my [Spanish postal codes project](https://dieghernan.github.io/projects/postal-codes-spain). The input data matters as much as the algorithm. With one representative point per code, Voronoi mainly maps distances between representatives. With address points, it can better approximate where each code's addresses are concentrated. It still knows nothing about delivery routes, physical barriers or official boundaries. We have not compared these results with an independent postal source for Slovenia. Before using them for analysis, we would need to review coverage, coordinates, the relationship with municipalities and sensitivity to the margins. For now, we have a working example that shows how the polygons are built, one step at a time. The title is a nod to Muse's album _Black Holes and Revelations_. ## References - Goerlich, F. J. (2022). _Elaboración de un mapa de códigos postales de España con recursos libres: Cómo evitar pagar por disponer de información de referencia_ (Working Paper No. 2022-3). Ivie. ([Updated online version](https://www.uv.es/goerlich/Ivie/CodPost.html)) - Hernangómez, D. (2026). _Códigos postales de España_ (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. ([Project documentation](https://dieghernan.github.io/codigospostales/)) - Pokojski, W., & Pokojska, P. (2018). Voronoi diagrams – Inventor, method, applications. _Polish Cartographical Review, 50_(3), 141–150. - Sánchez, J. I. (2020, November 13). Así hice el mapa de los códigos postales de España con SIG y datos abiertos. _Nosolosig_. [Article](https://www.nosolosig.com/articulos/asi-hice-el-mapa-de-los-codigos-postales-de-espana-con-sig-y-datos-abiertos)
entry.summary: From five imaginary points to a map of Slovenia: postal code areas with Voronoi, giscoR and sf.

entry.title: Postal codes of Spain
entry.content:
## Estimated postal code areas from open data ![](https://dieghernan.github.io/assets/img/misc/postal-codes-spain.jpg) [![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.23698418.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23698418) **Códigos postales de España** provides estimated postal code areas for Spain, built from open address data from [CartoCiudad](https://www.cartociudad.es/web/portal/) and administrative boundaries. Explore the results on interactive maps and download the data for use in **R**, **Python** or **QGIS**. ## Background Postal code polygons are useful for linking addresses and statistics to areas on a map. According to [Goerlich (2022)](https://doi.org/10.12842/WPIVIE_0322), the Correos polygons available through CartoCiudad stopped being offered for download in early 2017. This project explores a reproducible alternative based on open address data. An early reference is José Ignacio Sánchez's [2020 article in NoSoloSIG](https://www.nosolosig.com/articulos/asi-hice-el-mapa-de-los-codigos-postales-de-espana-con-sig-y-datos-abiertos), which describes how to estimate postal areas from CartoCiudad addresses using GIS tools. This project applies the approach developed in [Francisco José Goerlich's 2022 work](https://www.uv.es/goerlich/Ivie/CodPost.html), with its own choices for selecting addresses and handling areas without an assignment. ## Maps and data The [project website](https://dieghernan.github.io/codigospostales/) includes interactive maps and two GeoPackage downloads: a full version for spatial analysis and a simplified version for visualization. Both include postal code areas and administrative areas pending assignment. The data is shared under a [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). ### Interactive map Search for a postal code or address, select a two-digit prefix and compare the estimated areas with CartoCiudad. The viewer uses the simplified data and does not display areas pending assignment. Its controls are in Spanish.

Open the map in a full window Viewer guide

## Methodology Following Goerlich's approach, the workflow treats each separate component of an administrative area independently. When the selected addresses share a single postal code, it assigns that code to the whole component. When several codes are present, it builds Voronoi polygons around the address locations, clips them to the administrative boundary and merges areas with the same code. The final polygons are dissolved by postal code across provinces. This implementation selects addresses using an inward buffer of 200 m, with a second attempt at 50 m if none are found, rather than the 20 m described by Goerlich. Components without selected addresses remain unassigned unless the municipality has a single postal code recovered from its other components. The administrative boundaries come from [LAU2boundaries4Spain](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15345101), by Francisco José Goerlich and Pedro Pérez Vázquez. These are estimated areas, not official postal boundaries. Coverage depends on the source addresses and some areas remain unassigned. The [repository](https://github.com/dieghernan/codigospostales) documents the sources, methodology, limitations and steps to reproduce the data. ## References - Centro Nacional de Información Geográfica. (n.d.). *CartoCiudad* [Data set]. - Correos. (n.d.). *Base de datos de códigos postales y capa cartográfica* [Product information]. [Product page](https://www.correos.es/es/es/empresas/marketing/identifica-a-tus-clientes-potenciales/base-de-datos-de-codigos-postales) - Goerlich, F. J. (2022). *Elaboración de un mapa de códigos postales de España con recursos libres: Cómo evitar pagar por disponer de información de referencia* (Working Paper No. 2022-3). Ivie. ([Updated online version](https://www.uv.es/goerlich/Ivie/CodPost.html)) - Goerlich, F. J., & Pérez Vázquez, P. (2025). *Base de datos histórica de contornos municipales de España –LAU2boundaries4Spain–* (Version 2) [Data set]. Zenodo. - Hernangómez, D. (2026). *Códigos postales de España* (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. ([Project documentation](https://dieghernan.github.io/codigospostales/)) - Instituto Geográfico Nacional. (n.d.). *Servicios de visualización de CartoCiudad: Direcciones y códigos postales* [WMS documentation]. [Service documentation](https://www.cartociudad.es/web/portal/directorio-de-servicios/visualizacion) - Sánchez, J. I. (2020, November 13). Así hice el mapa de los códigos postales de España con SIG y datos abiertos. *Nosolosig*. [Article](https://www.nosolosig.com/articulos/asi-hice-el-mapa-de-los-codigos-postales-de-espana-con-sig-y-datos-abiertos)

entry.title: Large forest fires in Spain
entry.content:
## EGIF reports, reconciled fire records and cartography with R
![](https://dieghernan.github.io/assets/img/misc/gifs-social.jpg)
[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.23932940.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23932940)
**GIFs** brings together structured data on large forest fires in Spain and **R** code for an infographic inspired by [Dominic Royé's firefly cartography](https://dominicroye.github.io/blog/firefly-maps/). Here, GIF means *gran incendio forestal*: a fire with at least 500 hectares of forest area burned.
The project combines exports from MITECO's General Forest Fire Statistics (EGIF) with its annual reports and provisional updates. It preserves source information and reconciliation notes so that users can trace how records were selected, grouped and located.
![Large forest fires in Spain, 2010–2026. Dark map with orange circles sized by forest area burned.](https://dieghernan.github.io/gifs/gif_spain.png)
## Two related data products
The collection currently provides two complementary views:
- **EGIF reports:** 329 selected reports from 2010–2023. Each row has a unique `egif_part_id` and includes source fields, burned areas, cause, provenance, notes and coordinates where they can be interpreted. - **Reconciled fires:** 455 fire records from 2010–2026, used by the infographic. Each fire has a stable `fire_id`; a fire may bring together several EGIF reports.
These are different units of observation. Do not add the two tables' row counts or burned areas together. The 500-hectare threshold is applied after explicitly documented groupings of reports belonging to the same fire.
EGIF takes priority when a documented match exists. Records without a match retain their original MITECO annual report or provisional update. Reports awaiting reconciliation keep an empty `fire_id` and are not automatically added as new fires, which helps avoid double counting.
## Coverage and limitations
The fire-level records span February 27, 2010 to September 26, 2026. These are the first and last dates in the file, not evidence of complete annual coverage. The project is not a real-time monitoring service.
The documented reconciliation still has nine earlier fire records and eight selected EGIF reports awaiting a match. Two additional records retain their provisional source because their province has no reports in the 2023 EGIF export. That export contains no records for seven provinces, so an absence from these files should not be interpreted as an absence of fires.
The [methodology](https://github.com/dieghernan/gifs/blob/main/METODOLOGIA.md) explains source priority, explicit groupings and unresolved cases. The [data guide](https://github.com/dieghernan/gifs/blob/main/data-raw/README.md) documents the source exports and processing. The original ZIP files are preserved with SHA-256 checksums.
## Coordinates and the infographic
Geographic coordinates use EPSG:4326, keeping the Canary Islands in their actual location. EGIF coordinates are transformed only when their coordinate system can be interpreted. Missing coordinates or an unknown datum leave the geographic coordinates empty rather than producing an invented point.
The fire-level view uses interpretable EGIF coordinates where available and an identified municipal reference location otherwise. `location_method` distinguishes these sources. For fires with several reports, the view records which report supplies its reference point. Declared municipality codes and municipalities obtained through a spatial join are retained separately.
The points are reference locations, not fire perimeters. Municipal reference locations come from IGN through SIANE and **mapSpain**. The infographic reads the reconciled fire view and uses circle sizes to show forest area burned.
## Downloads, citation and reuse
Both products are available in **CSV**, **JSON** and **GeoJSON** from the [project website](https://dieghernan.github.io/gifs/). Read identifiers and municipality codes as text to preserve their representation. JSON supplies explicit types and null values; GeoJSON retains records without usable coordinates with `geometry: null`.
Machine-readable field descriptions are provided separately in the [EGIF report Croissant metadata](https://dieghernan.github.io/gifs/croissant/parts.json) and the [fire-level Croissant metadata](https://dieghernan.github.io/gifs/croissant/fires.json).
For reproducible analyses, cite the DOI of the version used. The collection's [version 2.0.0 DOI](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23932940) identifies the archived release; the [general DOI](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23929996) groups the project's releases.
Data reuse follows the [MITECO legal notice](https://www.miteco.gob.es/es/atencion-al-ciudadano/aviso-legal.html), including attribution and preservation of the original conditions and metadata. The municipal cartography credits CartoBase ANE 2006–2024, CC BY 4.0, IGN. The repository's MIT license applies to code and documentation. The project is independent and does not imply MITECO participation or endorsement.
## References
- Royé, D. (2021, June 1). Firefly cartography. *Dr Dominic Royé*. <https://dominicroye.github.io/blog/firefly-maps/>

entry.title: Let’s peel the world
entry.content: ## Do you know the interrupted Goode homolosine projection? ![](https://dieghernan.github.io/assets/img/blog/202610_goode-map-1.webp) What would happen if we peeled the Earth like an orange? The [interrupted Goode homolosine projection](https://proj.org/en/stable/operations/projections/igh.html) gives us something close to that! This equal-area projection preserves relative areas while splitting the world map into lobes. Add a few shades of orange and our world is ready to peel. Let's make it with **sf**, **giscoR** and **ggplot2**. First, we get the coastlines and draw the outline, following the cuts between the lobes. ```r library(sf) library(ggplot2) library(giscoR) library(showtext) world <- gisco_get_coastal_lines(resolution = 10) goode_crs <- "+proj=igh" lat <- c(90:-90, rep(c(-90:0, 0:-90), 3), -90:90, 90:0, 0:90, 90) lon <- c( rep(180, 181), rep(c(80.01, 79.99, -19.99, -20.01, -99.99, -100.01), each = 91), rep(-180, 181), rep(c(-40.01, -39.99), each = 91), 180 ) outline <- st_sfc(st_polygon(list(cbind(lon, lat))), crs = 4326) |> st_transform(goode_crs) rectangle <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(outline) * 1.1) mask <- st_difference(rectangle, outline) ``` Next, we draw the meridians and parallels within each lobe so that they do not connect across the cuts. ```r lobes <- list( c(-180, -40, 0, 90), c(-40, 180, 0, 90), c(-180, -100, -90, 0), c(-100, -20, -90, 0), c(-20, 80, -90, 0), c(80, 180, -90, 0) ) lines <- lapply(lobes, function(b) { west <- b[1] + 0.01 east <- b[2] - 0.01 south <- max(b[3], -89.99) north <- min(b[4], 89.99) meridians <- seq(-180, 180, 30) meridians <- meridians[meridians > west & meridians < east] parallels <- seq(-60, 60, 30) parallels <- parallels[parallels >= south & parallels <= north] c( lapply(meridians, function(x) { st_linestring(cbind(x, seq(south, north, length.out = 181))) }), lapply(parallels, function(y) { st_linestring(cbind(seq(west, east, length.out = 361), y)) }) ) }) grat <- st_sfc(do.call(c, lines), crs = 4326) |> st_transform(goode_crs) ``` Finally, we add the orange palette. The mask hides anything outside the outline and keeps the edges of our peel tidy. ```r font_add_google("Coiny", family = "coiny") showtext_auto() ggplot() + geom_sf(data = outline, fill = "#FFF0D9", colour = NA) + geom_sf(data = world, fill = "#F9B566", colour = "#B34D08", linewidth = 0.25) + geom_sf(data = grat, fill = NA, colour = "#E8A45B", linewidth = 0.25) + geom_sf(data = mask, fill = "#fcf1e7", colour = NA) + geom_sf(data = outline, fill = NA, colour = "#E87516", linewidth = 0.4) + coord_sf( crs = goode_crs, xlim = st_bbox(outline)[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = st_bbox(outline)[c("ymin", "ymax")], expand = FALSE, datum = NA ) + theme_void() + theme( text = element_text(family = "coiny"), plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#fcf1e7", colour = NA), plot.title = element_text( color = "#E87516", face = "bold", size = rel(3), margin = margin(b = 10) ), plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10), plot.caption = element_text( color = "#E87516", size = rel(1.5), margin = margin(t = 10) ) ) + labs( title = "Let's peel the world", caption = "Interrupted Goode homolosine projection" ) ``` ## References - Panaïotis, T. (2026, September 29). Projections cartographiques : Le guide pour ne pas y laisser sa santé mentale. _Pyranhia_. [Article](https://pyranhia.eu/posts/202609-carto-proj-avancees/carto-proj-avancees.html) - Wilke, C. O. (n.d.). _Interrupted Goode homolosine_. practicalgg. (Source for the outline and masking approach.)
entry.summary: Peel the world like an orange with the interrupted Goode homolosine projection and draw it in R.

entry.title: Conversations across the web with Webmentions

link.title: Conversations across the web with Webmentions

entry.content:
## Bringing mentions, likes and reposts back to the blog ![](https://dieghernan.github.io/assets/img/blog/202610-webmentions-header.webp) Conversations about a blog post often happen somewhere else. Someone shares a link, replies on their own site or reacts to a post on social media. I wanted to bring some of that activity back here. This implementation was directly inspired by **Matt Hobbs's** article, [Implementing Webmentions on this blog](https://nooshu.com/blog/2019/11/18/implementing-webmentions/), published on **Nooshu**. I liked its simple presentation: links to mentions and replies, followed by small groups of avatars for likes and reposts. So I added a similar section to this blog, using the typography, colors and buttons from [Chulapa](https://dieghernan.github.io/chulapa). ## How it works A [Webmention](https://www.w3.org/TR/webmention/) is a notification that one page links to another. If you write about one of my posts on your own site, you can send its URL so the link can appear below the original article. This blog already advertised a [**Webmention.io**](https://webmention.io/) endpoint. The missing piece was displaying the mentions it had collected. A small JavaScript file now requests the public mentions for each post's canonical URL and builds the section automatically when the page opens. Mentions and replies appear as a numbered list of links and authors. Likes and reposts have their own counts and rows of overlapping avatars. The content stays on its original site. Each link takes you to the conversation. The existing GitHub comments are still available, too. ## A small addition to a static blog The implementation uses a Jekyll include, a stylesheet and plain JavaScript. There is no extra Jekyll plugin or change to the deployment workflow. **Webmention.io** handles receiving and verifying links, while the browser loads the results through its public API. I tried it with the [geobounds post]({% post_url 2026-02-12-geobounds %}), which already had mentions, and with a recent post that had none. Both cases matter: an empty section should still explain how to join in. Sharing a link on a social network only brings reactions here if a bridge sends them as Webmentions. ## Send a link Written something that links to this post? Open **Shared your thoughts on this post? Drop your link here!** below and submit your page's URL. The form works without JavaScript, although displaying existing mentions requires it. Thanks to **Matt Hobbs** for the inspiration and for sharing his [implementation](https://gist.github.com/Nooshu/121e5bf7f3d5c6528413c57db257894f). It is a nice way to let a static blog take part in a wider conversation.

AI assistance: I wrote this post with help from Codex, including drafting and editing the text. Codex also helped implement and test the Webmentions section. The header image was also generated with AI.
entry.summary: A small addition to my Jekyll blog, inspired by Matt Hobbs: Webmentions with a Chulapa look.
